items.body: Run by our very own Joseph Sannicandro, the Lost Children Net Label has been quiet as a Bandcamp imprint, but kept alive through Joseph’s podcasts and newsletter posts since the 2022 release of the massive 56-track [Useless Sounds]. Returning in full force with a triptych of tapes, Lost Children is ready to reclaim its place at the forefront of experimental music. The crown jewel of the bundle is CRACKS, a gathering of international musicians who address the “concept of the border as a colonial wound.” Proceeds benefit the Council on American-Islamic Relations Minnesota and Lumpen Radio (an initiative of the Public Media Institute in Chicago). The confrontational words on the cover have become a global rallying cry. Joni Void starts the set off with “Borders,” cutting right to the chase. The percussion sounds like a jailer’s baton dragged across prison bars. A connection is made between physical borders, sonic borders and the borders of perception, with dialogue interrupted by the siren and blare of a local enforcement agent. Martín Rodríguez shares radio transmissions heard from the Arizona-Mexico border where he was raised, giving credit to radio for helping him to recover from a brain tumor. The transmissions sparkle and fade, as if underlining the name of the Lost Children imprint. One thinks of voices and souls lost and the search for missing loved ones, possibly deported, possibly dead. Kate Carr offers bucolic bells bisected by the essential chaos of street protests, suggesting that the comfortable must be disturbed in order for substantive change to unfold. Lubo Alexandrov‘s bucolic “Echoes (from the other side)” doesn’t identify which side it refers to, leaving the interpretation wide open. Speaker Music‘s haunting, echoed, abraded and ultimately percussive “Moral Injury” exposes the deepest rupture of the crisis as an affront to goodness itself. Sannicandro’s own “rethink not reform” brings the sound to the streets, the appealing “Wait” of an electronic crossing signal contrasted with a sense that the fragile peace is about to be disturbed; in layers of increasing ferocity, it is. The disorientation of the intimate soundscape imitates that of the assaulted. apartment52‘s “i would die for anything, maybe” exposes a different insecurity while repeating the effect of messages that fail to get through. A heartfelt live recording from Hamza Lahmadi connects the yearning of sojourners around the world, who just want a place to call home. Mai Mai Mai incorporates waves as siren call, implying both the hope of welcome and the lack of permission to land. The drone is lonely and isolated, the land right there. Anas Hajam lightens the mood a bit with finger-picking goodness and breath; one needs encouragement such as this. Then Joni Void returns as the remixer of Soledad Rosas‘ “Piel,” which extends the references to breath along with vocal glissandos and tender song. The intake just prior to the second minute recalls George Floyd. Only a minute long, Esther B.‘s “molti sport” is a rush of static awaiting definition. Then comes a reference to Greek mythology: thenewobjective feat. Cole Pulice use “Scylla and Charybdis” to reference the idiom “the lesser of two evils,” summarizing the current state of border disputes, in which no one wins. Stefan Christoff closes the compilation with “Turn,” whose tolling church bells, echoed on prepared piano, are both indictment and call to arms. Two artists featured on CRACKS also branch out across the bundle. ATMOSPHERICS is taken from a series of soundscape broadcasts prepared by Diana Duta & Stefan Christoff. Partially recorded on the silver anniversary of Portugal’s Carnation Revolution, “Paysage sonare” is a tribute to victory, a long battle finally won. The sounds of the coast are sounds of peace in both senses of the word. Soft ambient tones unify the composition, wresting control from the field recordings in the tenth minute before ceding space in the eighteenth and again in the thirty-first, ending in familial laughter and joy. Similar sounds launch the title track, recorded in Brussels. The piece eventually branches into the northern marshes, calling on hydrophones for a glance below the surface. The contrast between city and marsh recalls CRACKS: the discussion of desirable environments, “migration, political dissent and resistance.” The link becomes overt in the chants of the twenty-first minute. Again Christoff’s synth, along with pensive guitar, is the glue that holds the work together, although even this is lost in time, rescued from older tapes, a subtle metaphor. In the long aquatic segment that closes the piece, one feels retreat and resolution. Esther B. is also Esther Bourdages, whose cassette Listening session, live concerts, figure skating “turns the turntable into a destructive instrument.” These live improvisations expose the turntable as preserver and destroyer of memory. Segments rise through the ether intact, only to be savaged with love. There’s a huge difference between turntablism in a hip-hop sense and turntablism in an experimental sense, but the two are not exclusive. In her preference for the older, even archival records, Bourdages honors The Caretaker; in her disdain for the creation of linear narratives or danceable samples, she honors Kid Koala. “figure skating” flips the script, conflating the stylus and the skate, the vinyl and the ice, with few if any identifiable markers until the end: a mesmerizing lesson in abstraction and a companion to Curling. In “Earache, My Eye,” a horrified son protests to his father, “You ruined my record, man!” Such a thing does not exist in Bourdages’ world, where records are purposely altered by “grinding, cutting and sanding.” If anything, the imperfections are the draw. Yet it is obvious that the artist loves her collection, teasing sounds from these records that were never intended to be heard, like coaxing stories from a childhood friend. It is passing strange to hear them on a cassette, although in the hands of another this might be manipulated in a different way, then passed to a digital specialist for further dismantling. We once thought that sound, once recorded, was fixed; we believe so no longer. Welcome back, Lost Children! (Richard Allen)

You will search in vain for rhythms and harmonies here, of course; "Gold" is an album of free form. It chirps, pings and creaks merrily away; only in track 12 (the tracks have no titles) does something almost akin to a dance mood arise as a result of the electronic percussion; although even to this you can hardly dance, there is simply too much going on. An oriental-sounding flute improvises over heavy chirping and bubbling above the quasi-soloing percussion. Space techno? With the following track, "13", which sounds like a cool, empty factory hall turned into music, a bit of Industrial also comes into play."Gold" is fun and enormously entertaining for those people who (like me) find many of the productions of the "Berlin School" incredibly boring. Not a typical Conrad Schnitzler album, but for me (perhaps for that very reason) one of the best.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — ProjeKct Three's 'Masque' comes straight from the R&D department of King Crimson. This is the thirdinstallment in the live project series featuring members of the 'THRAK' lineup of the Robert Fripp-led band, brought together with the aim of exploring off-beat ideas through improvisation andexperimentation. These are live recordings featuring alternating lineups of the 90s Crimson, withthis particular 1999 recording featuring the trio of Robert Fripp, Trey Gunn, and Pat Mastelotto. Asis the case with the majority of the KC releases from that period, the music played by ProjeKctThree incorporates the spacey ambient soundscapes patented by Fripp, together with the finely tunedWarr guitar of Trey Gunn and the impressive array of electronic percussion and loops played by PatMastelotto. The type of experimental rock presented on 'Masque', however, is more abstract and lessgroovy than the output of other ProjeKcts (like One or Two, which makes it closer to something like'Thrakattak' than the album 'THRAK' itself.The thirteen tracks making up this live album are numbered and (perhaps suggestively) left untitled,while the somewhat intimidating, surreal and impersonal cover art uncannily reflects the kind ofmusic played on 'Masque'. This is one of these experimental recordings that only make sense whenheard in their entirety, but if I were to outline several pieces of greater significance, I wouldhave to start with '1', which is an obnoxious and impulsive opener, replete with hefty bass tonesand obscure guitar licks. 'Masque 2' then presents a more sustained rock sound tinted with gentleambient soundscapes, while the complex rhythms on '3' weave around the haunting electronics in arather menacing way. Later on, 'Masque 7' represents another abstract-sided piece, impressing with asoft but prominent bass sound, whereas the industrial hue encompassing 'Masque 8' makes it one ofthe darker compositions heard on this album. It is also worth noting how effective the hypnoticallyabrasive sounds on '9' are, with the two final pieces also being among the highlights.Of all the ProjeKcts, Three might be the single most intriguing variation of Crimson - 'Masque' isunorthodox and compelling, but for me this is the kind of experimentation that drives the genreforward.

items.body: Impressed by this partnership’s Dvořák Ninth (review), I was eager to hear their Bruckner fourth, surely the composer’s most popular symphony both in the concert hall and on record. This new reading, while impressive, is not a complete success. Symphony No. 4 Amazon Presto Apple This reading lacks the instrumental weight and depth of color that I would argue makes for an authentic Bruckner sound. Having grown up listening to many Telarc recordings of this orchestra, I lay the blame for this deficiency on the engineering. The mics are placed too close to the musicians, surely to minimize audience noise during this live recording. There is little bloom to the sound, and no real hall ambience. Climaxes feel contained, and softer dynamics are limited by the proximity of the mics. Bruckner’s music was written with a warm, reverberant acoustic in mind, and that acoustic is an integral part of the sound. Not so here. Instead, it is like standing one foot away from Seurat’s A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte: every brush stroke is visible, and we might appreciate how the painting is assembled, but it comes at the cost of the image’s beauty, mystery and expression. The second issue has to do with the edition. There are now ten different editions of the fourth symphony to choose from. Stutzmann uses the late Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs’ 2021 critical edition of the 1878–81 version, which has been recorded only once before, by Simon Rattle with the LSO (LSO Live). For that album Cohrs described his edition as “the second version of the ‘Romantic’ Symphony as it stood by the end of 1881,” including “Bruckner’s own suggested cut in the Finale.” But Stutzmann does not take the cut — why not? Why embrace a little-known version and then ignore one of its most significant, composer-sanctioned changes? The liner notes offer no discussion of the edition, nor is it listed on either side of the booklet cover. As to the performance itself, I had initially intended to limit comparisons to other American recordings, but it now seems best to set Stutzmann against Rattle (details – review). His performance is faster, with an overall timing of 61’30” against Stutzmann’s 71’39”, and the largest difference comes in the final movement, where Stutzmann restores the passage Bruckner marked for cutting. Each conductor belongs to a different interpretive school. Rattle recalls Karajan: a subtle use of rubato, polished orchestral sound with resplendent brass and gossamer strings, a unified pulse that keeps the structure in view. Stutzmann is far closer to Jochum: much freer rubato, a more heterogeneous orchestral sound and, more distinctively, an intensely songful rendering of Bruckner’s score. Nathalie Stutzmann conducts the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra. Photo © Rand Lines. Stutzmann’s approach is compelling in the second movement, though at 17’05” it feels more Adagio than Bruckner’s Andante quasi Allegretto. In the finale the flexibility sometimes compromises a sense of the overarching structure, and there are moments when the energy level dips precipitously low. This is less of an issue in the opening movement, where one does get to hear much of the contrapuntal inner voices. Both Rattle and Stutzmann solicit rounded articulation, and I often missed the cut and thrust of Blomstedt’s San Francisco account on Decca and Honeck’s Pittsburgh performance on Reference, especially in the Scherzo. Both drive the music harder, encouraging more wildness in the trumpet-capped climaxes. Bruckner described the Trio as “how a barrel-organ plays during the midday meal in the forest.” Honeck is perhaps best at capturing this rustic picture, even if he is reticent to allow an earthier, less refined sound. Stutzmann conjures a poised, lightly sprung elegance that I enjoyed, even though it hardly captures the composer’s description. In short, I find Stutzmann’s performance the more compelling of the two. Yet if I want to hear this edition, surely I want Bruckner’s cut in the finale. Rattle’s release adds to the symphony itself the discarded 1874/76 Scherzo and the 1878 Volksfest Finale, an extended early version of the Andante, and the unabridged 1881 Finale, a valuable addition for Bruckner specialists. Ultimately, neither recording compels me to embrace this version over the more familiar Haas and Nowak editions, and neither matches the brilliance of Blomstedt, Honeck, or the classic Böhm/Vienna/Decca. items.body: Mitsuko Uchida’s 2025 live performance of the late Beethoven sonatas (Op. 109–111) arrives almost two decades after her studio recording for Decca, and it carries the added weight of being her final account of these works. Her choice of Suntory Hall marks a homecoming: she has played there since the hall’s opening season in 1986, and remains its only Associate Artist. Last Three Sonatas Amazon Presto Apple The gap between the two readings naturally raises the question of how much her interpretations have developed. If we go by Op. 109, things have indeed changed: not a drastic pivot, but an amplification of certain aspects. The 2006 reading already had an appreciable fluidity, but in the newer Vivace (track 1) Uchida makes more unabashed pauses and rubatos that still fit naturally into the music. Some of the urgency of the earlier second movement has turned into greater dramatic power here, and the attention to articulation and secondary voices is never sacrificed. The temperament of the final movement (track 3) can vary considerably depending on the tempo of the opening theme. Where Serkin and Gilels move more slowly and evoke contemplation, Uchida is brisker than either of them, and her pace captures the cantabile of Beethoven’s marking. In the variations that follow, a deep familiarity reveals itself in her ability to balance forward motion against the emphasis the grandest moments need. Op. 110 comes alive through contrast. Uchida uses Beethoven’s textures to shift between lyricism and resonance. The arpeggios at the start of the Moderato cantabile (track 4), leading up to the second theme, are a prime example: they begin as shimmering filigree and morph into a resplendent presence — perhaps a fitting representation of the vocal and orchestral sides she brings out throughout. The Scherzo carries a much higher degree of austerity and insistence than the 2006 Decca version, though both readings remain entirely valid. The Adagio (track 6) reveals a performer who understands the profundity of late Beethoven: the desperation, the melancholy with its sharp poignancy, the gravitas of internal conflict and weariness. What is most captivating is her ability to convey the rawness of these sentiments in a live setting. Uchida’s Fuga (track 7) proves more multidimensional than many. The switch from minor to major is subtle, and it gives her room to explore the quieter sides of the fugue before it spins into something much larger. Even in the softest playing nothing sounds hurried. Pauses are placed to maximize dynamic contrast while delineating the intricacies of Beethoven’s structure. Mitsuko Uchida. Photo © Justin Pumfrey / Decca. Although it moves slightly slower at times than her previous interpretation, the new Op. 111 (tracks 8–9) embodies the severity and boldness of the Maestoso marking. The urgency of the prior account has developed into an equally compelling adamance. The calmness of the Arietta feels like an arrival after a long journey. The same weighty substance carries into the variations, which works for the most part, though the syncopated variation at 6’40” could take a touch more rhythmic vitality. What emerges most strongly, though, is the intricacy of the tender moments, which linger in their transcendence. The engineers have kept audience noise to a minimum, and the piano is captured with enough clarity to register its tone and regulation. As a final account of these sonatas this is a distinguished one, and the culmination of Uchida’s long engagement with them. items.body: Saint-Saëns completed his Symphony No. 3 in 1886, commissioned by the Philharmonic Society of London, and conducted the premiere himself at the age of fifty. It was the last symphony he would write, and it came at the height of his career. He is said to have remarked that he would never achieve anything like it again. When Franz Liszt died later that year, Saint-Saëns dedicated the score to his memory. The “Organ” nickname is a little misleading. The composer wrote not a concerto but a symphony “with organ,” where the instrument works inside the orchestra rather than in front of it. The scoring also calls for a piano, played at times by two players. The four traditional movements are folded into two continuous parts, unified by a single theme that keeps returning in new forms, a technique absorbed from Liszt. The music travels from restless C minor to a blazing C major finale, whose massive organ entrance has tested engineers as much as conductors. Recordings have answered that challenge in different ways, from concert-hall organs captured in place to a cathedral instrument recorded separately and mixed in. Here are The Classic Review editorial team’s recommendations for the best recordings of Saint-Saëns’s Symphony No. 3 (“Organ”). Boston Symphony Orchestra, Charles Munch More than sixty years after it was made, Charles Munch’s 1959 recording in Boston remains the one to beat. The thrill comes from playing of scorching intensity that unfolds like a live concert. Munch sets a fast tempo for the first movement’s main theme, and the rhythmic drive never lets up. The strings sing the *Poco adagio* with unforced lyricism, a reminder that this performance is not all fire. In the finale, Berj Zamkochian’s organ makes a thunderous entrance, its bass seeming to shake the floor. The aging tape strains audibly under that huge chord, yet the drama sweeps this flaw aside. Add Munch’s Debussy *La Mer* and Ibert *Escales* as couplings, and the disc’s legendary status is easy to understand. Munch Amazon Presto Apple Chicago Symphony Orchestra, Daniel Barenboim The organ heard on Daniel Barenboim’s 1976 Chicago recording was played an ocean away from the orchestra. Gaston Litaize recorded his part on the organ of Chartres Cathedral, and the two performances were joined afterward in the studio. That procedure could easily have sounded artificial, but the combined result has an epic, almost otherworldly presence. It crowns a performance of irresistible panache, with the Chicago brass playing at full strength and a finale of colossal impact. Barenboim’s invigorating first-movement tempo leaves the strings a little untidy in places, a small price for the sweep he achieves. It matches Munch for voltage while sounding far more modern. For the symphony’s raw physical thrill, this is the version to reach for. Barenboim Amazon Presto Apple Detroit Symphony Orchestra, Paul Paray Paul Paray’s 1957 Detroit account moves with exceptional lightness. Its appeal is not weight or blaze, but transparency and grace. Paray trained this orchestra himself, and it shows in the supple phrasing and the way every strand stays audible. Tempos are bracingly fast, yet nothing feels rushed. The playing stays composed even at full speed. The organ part is in the hands of Marcel Dupré, one of the great virtuosos of the twentieth century. Made with just three microphones, the recording remains astonishingly fresh for its age, clearer than Munch’s. For listeners who want to hear the elegance inside this symphony, Paray is the essential alternative. Paray Amazon Presto Apple Montreal Symphony Orchestra, Charles Dutoit Few discs did more to show off the young CD format than Charles Dutoit’s 1982 Montreal recording. Its lasting virtues, though, are musical: elastic, beautifully controlled phrasing and orchestral playing of rare polish. Peter Hurford’s organ is cleanly focused and never distorts, even in the loudest pages. Every detail sits in natural proportion. The coupling is the Second Piano Concerto, with Pascal Rogé as soloist. Those who crave the sheer force of Munch or Barenboim may find Dutoit reserved. Anyone meeting the symphony for the first time could not ask for a better guide. Dutoit Amazon Presto Apple Kansas City Symphony, Michael Stern Glorious sound is the first thing anyone notices about Michael Stern’s 2013 recording with the Kansas City Symphony. It is not, however, the main reason to recommend the album. The performance underneath has genuine vitality, with crisp rhythms and the rich, full-bodied sonority this music thrives on. Jan Kraybill presides over a big Casavant concert organ, and the recording gives it impressive depth and space. The couplings are generous: the *Introduction and Rondo capriccioso* with violinist Noah Geller, and the lesser-known *La Muse et le Poète*. A performance this alive earns its place beside the classics. Stern Amazon Presto Apple Top image ©️ The Classic Review, AI generated The form can be filled in the actual website url. items.body: The members of the Norwegian trio Tazer introduce themselves only by their aliases: ‘CALICO’, ‘ONI-X01’, and ‘DRUMNIBAL’. Beyond that, they prefer to keep an air of mystery – something I won’t attempt to unravel here. Their focus is on the music rather than the people behind it, and rightly so. I first discovered Tazer through their earlier EP, but it is their self-released debut album, “Taze Is The Rule”, that truly demands attention. It has been a long time since a debut record has hit me with this kind of force. This is pure sonic aggression, forged from a relentless fusion of EBM, Metal, and Techno. Every track is crushingly heavy, leaving nothing standing in its wake. The songs strike with the intensity of an imaginary war machine, determined to conquer dark dance floors and every poor soul brave enough to step onto them. Tazer sounds like an explosion whose full impact has yet to be measured. Fortunately, the band took the time to answer a few questions and shed some light on the ideas, influences, and vision behind “Taze Is The Rule”. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Tazer ‘Taze Is The Rule’ interview Q: Let’s start by clearing up a few things: where do Tazer and the project’s name come from? Who is behind the aliases, and what has your musical journey been like up to this point? CALICO: The Tazer project officially kicked off in 2024 when we wrote our first EP, “9001 Volts”. We chose the name Tazer because we wanted something that felt high-voltage but was also instantly recognizable. A small taser can pack a massive punch, and that just felt like the perfect metaphor for our energy. As for our aliases, they are symbols. Honestly, who we are behind them really doesn’t matter, we are our music, and we prefer to let the tracks do the talking. Q: What have been the key influences and sources of inspiration behind your music, and what does this particular form of expression mean to you? ONI-X01: We’ve always been massive fans of bands like Rammstein and Combichrist, but we really wanted to inject our own flavor into the mix. The goal was to create something heavy and raw, but also immediate and danceable. By mixing Metal with classic EBM elements, we want to hit people right in the gut and pull them into a completely new kind of mindset. Q: How did this debut album come together, and how were the songwriting and production responsibilities divided among the band members? Looking back, what were the biggest challenges you faced while creating it? DRUMNIBAL: This album is the result of years of hard work. Out of the 10 tracks we originally wrote, 5 of them ended up on the “9001 Volts” EP. So, over the next two years, we had to write 5 brand-new tracks to bring the album back to 10. During that time, our sound naturally evolved and the line-up shifted into the trio we are today. Lyrics always come last because they depend entirely on the vibe and emotion the music triggers in us. We write everything together as a team, no strict division of labor, just pure collaboration. Both lyrically and musically, the track comes across as hard-hitting, provocative, and uncompromising. Could you elaborate on that? However, with this specific project, we are completely rethinking our approach to live shows to deliver something genuinely fresh and powerful. We know it’s a challenge, ‘cause the live scene is incredibly competitive right now, and coming up with original ideas takes a lot of the discipline we talk about. We apply that same focus to our music videos, carefully crafting our identity through every choice of makeup, wardrobe, storyline, and camera angle. Q: Are you already working on new material or perhaps even a follow-up album? Do you have a clear vision of how Tazer will evolve in the future and where you would like to take the project? CALICO: We definitely have a long-term plan, which includes diving into a second album. We already have some ideas cooking that we hope people will love. Right now, though, the main focus of that plan is locking down and developing our live shows. We honestly can’t wait to bring these tracks to the stage and connect with the crowd under the banner of ‘Taze is the Rule’. About Tazer Tazer is a Norwegian electro-industrial project formed in 2024 by musicians performing under the aliases CALICO, ONI-X01, and DRUMNIBAL, and signed to Hellektrokution Records. The band debuted with the single “A Razor Can Slit, A Tazer Can Kill” on 5 November 2024, followed by the self-released EP “9001 Volts” on 21 December 2024. Of the ten tracks the band had written by then, five appeared on that EP; the remaining five, plus five newly written tracks, became the ten-track debut album “Taze Is The Rule”, released via Hellektrokution Records on 30 April 2026. The album combines EBM, industrial metal and techno, with influences including Rammstein and Combichrist. Tazer returned in October 2025 with a Halloween video for “I Put a Spell on You”, and in May 2026 released the single “Raise The Voltage”, the album’s fifth track, via Hellektrokution Records, Spotify, YouTube and Bandcamp. The band is now focused on developing a live show and has begun writing material for a second album.

The video, titled “A-Ha – Hunting High And Low, if it was recorded in the 50s,” runs 30 minutes and 20 seconds and covers the album’s full ten-track sequence, including “Take On Me.” The video was already uploaded on November 10, 2025, and has drawn 5,345 views so far. Not a lot that is, despite being one of the better produced videos on his channel, musically speaking. The vocal performance is not Morten Harket’s, and the channel is upfront about the nature of the project, opening with a disclaimer that “voices, faces and characters have no connection to actual people”, and that “the video is an artistic and transformative work made for entertainment purposes.” A recurring format built around AI reinterpretation marceve76 runs a 51,900-subscriber channel built almost entirely around reimagining well-known albums as 1950s recordings, a format that leans on AI music generation, voice and style transfer. Side-Line covered the same creator’s take on Depeche Mode’s “Violator” in July 2025. The “Hunting High and Low” video sits in the same catalog alongside similar treatments of Fleetwood Mac’s “Rumours,” Blondie’s “Parallel Lines,” David Bowie’s “Let’s Dance,” Led Zeppelin’s debut, Dio’s “Holy Diver” and AC/DC’s “The Razors Edge,” among others. The full “Hunting High and Low” tracklist covered in the video, with timestamps: “Take On Me” – 0:00 “Train of Thought” – 2:52 “Hunting High and Low” – 5:52 “The Blue Sky” – 9:09 “Living a Boy’s Adventure Tale” – 12:18 “The Sun Always Shines on T.V.” – 16:12 “And You Tell Me” – 19:44 “Love Is Reason” – 22:20 “I Dream Myself Alive” – 24:52 “Here I Stand and Face the Rain” – 27:17 About a-ha a-ha formed in Oslo, Norway, in 1982, when vocalist Morten Harket joined songwriters Pål Waaktaar and Magne Furuholmen, who had been playing together in earlier Oslo bands. Signed to Warner Bros., the trio released their debut album, “Hunting High and Low,” on June 1, 1985, in Norway and the United States, followed by a UK and European release on October 28 that year. Its lead single “Take On Me” had first been issued in 1984 without success; a 1985 re-release, paired with Steve Barron’s rotoscope-animated video mixing live action and pencil animation, took the song to number one in 36 countries and won six awards at the 1986 MTV Video Music Awards. “Hunting High and Low” also produced the singles “Love Is Reason,” “The Sun Always Shines on T.V.,” “Train of Thought” and the title track. The album has remained a recurring point of reference for the band’s reissue campaigns: Side-Line reported on a 6LP boxset built around the record in January 2023, and on an exclusive 1984 Demos vinyl pressed for Record Store Day 2025. a-ha went on to release albums including “Scoundrel Days” (1986), “Stay on These Roads” (1988), “East of the Sun, West of the Moon” (1990), “Memorial Beach” (1993), and, after a 2000s reunion, “Analogue” (2005), “Foot of the Mountain” (2009), “Cast in Steel” (2015) and “True North” (2022), the latter accompanied by a documentary film. Side-Line covered the 20th-anniversary reissue of “Analogue” as a 2CD deluxe set with a first-time vinyl pressing in February 2026. In June 2025, Morten Harket revealed a Parkinson’s diagnosis, and Magne Furuholmen discussed the band’s creative process in a Side-Line interview earlier that year. “Take On Me” itself continues to draw new versions from other artists, including a 2025 dark cover by Pure Obsessions & Red Nights.

items.body: English post-punk band The Cure may release their fifteenth studio album in November 2026, according to an unconfirmed report. French fan site Pictures of Cure published the claim on July 31, 2026, citing an unnamed source inside Universal, the band’s distributor, who reportedly listed the album in the company’s release schedule for that month. The report was relayed the same day on the fan forum curefans.com, in its “Unconfirmed news and rumours” section. Neither The Cure, frontman Robert Smith, nor Universal has confirmed a release date. Pictures of Cure ties the November claim to two earlier data points: Smith’s remarks during a BBC Radio 6 Music interview recorded on June 6, 2026, in which he said the album was about to be delivered to the label, and the fact that “Songs of a Lost World,” the record Smith has repeatedly described as this album’s companion piece, was released on November 1, 2024. What Robert Smith has said about the album The Cure returned to Rockfield Studios in Wales in March 2025 to record what Smith has described as three albums’ worth of material. Side-Line reported at the time that 13 songs had been recorded. In the June 2026 BBC Radio 6 Music interview, Smith said the second of those three albums is finished and being delivered to Universal. He called it “more dismal than Songs Of A Lost World” and said it is emotionally connected to that album while approaching the material from a different perspective. A third album, drawn from the same sessions, is “really, really upbeat” and “really poppy,” Smith said, with no indication yet of when it might follow. Two songs earmarked for the upcoming album were named by Smith in January 2025: “It Can Never Be the Same,” a song about grief that the band has performed live for years under the earlier title “Christmas Without You,” and “A Boy I Never Knew,” written during the sessions for The Cure’s 2004 self-titled album. Smith has said the album will also include newer, previously unheard material. “Songs of a Lost World” was released on November 1, 2024, through Fiction Records, ending a 16-year gap since “4:13 Dream” (2008). Produced and mixed by Smith with Paul Corkett and recorded at Rockfield Studios, it was the first Cure album written entirely by Smith and gave the band its first UK number one album in 32 years. About The Cure The Cure formed in Crawley, West Sussex, England, in January 1976, when school friends Robert Smith and Michael Dempsey began playing together, initially under the name Malice. The band went through the name Easy Cure before settling on The Cure and signing to Fiction Records, distributed by Polydor, in 1978. The founding lineup of Smith (guitar, vocals), Dempsey (bass) and Lol Tolhurst (drums) released the debut album “Three Imaginary Boys” in 1979. Through numerous lineup changes, with Smith as the only constant member, The Cure built a catalogue running from the austere post-punk of “Seventeen Seconds” (1980) and “Faith” (1981) through “Pornography” (1982), the pop-facing “The Head on the Door” (1985) and “Kiss Me, Kiss Me, Kiss Me” (1987), to “Disintegration” (1989) and “Wish” (1992), among later releases including “Wild Mood Swings” (1996), “Bloodflowers” (2000), the self-titled “The Cure” (2004) and “4:13 Dream” (2008). The current lineup comprises Robert Smith, Simon Gallup (bass), Roger O’Donnell (keyboards), Jason Cooper (drums) and Reeves Gabrels (guitar). Guitarist and keyboardist Perry Bamonte, who first joined the band in 1984 and rejoined for the “Shows of a Lost World” tour in 2022, died in December 2025 at age 65. The band returned after 16 years away from new albums with “Songs of a Lost World” on November 1, 2024, and confirmed in October 2025 that a follow-up had been recorded at Rockfield Studios. The unconfirmed report of a November 2026 release date would place a new Cure album exactly two years after its predecessor.

items.body: It took the Norwegian duo Kant Kino nearly nine years to release their fourth album. Despite this lengthy hiatus, EBM fans are unlikely to have forgotten the band, as their previous full-length releases were polished, expertly crafted examples of the genre. While EBM remains the album’s primary influence, “Echoes Of The End” also ventures into other sonic territories. The result is a compelling fusion of EBM and Electro-Pop, with occasional touches of Future-Pop. Some tracks recall the melodic approach of Assemblage 23, while the album’s darker moments evoke the early work of Skinny Puppy. At its core, however, “Echoes Of The End” remains a hard-hitting, relentless EBM record, impeccably executed and enriched with vintage-inspired synth textures. The powerful yet controlled vocal delivery perfectly complements the album’s atmosphere. We are treated to no fewer than 24 tracks, although for me the collection is ultimately defined by the irresistible “Choice.” Kant Kino is back—and not a moment too soon. While their sound has evolved, they continue to deliver EBM of the highest caliber. (Rating:8½). Side-Line previously covered the announcement of “Echoes of The End” in April 2026, when the album was confirmed as a digital deluxe edition and a physical 2CD via Alfa Matrix. Listen to “Choice”: Choice by Kant Kino About Kant Kino Kant Kino is a Norwegian electronic duo from Oslo, namely Lars Henrik Madsen and Kenneth Fredstie. The project formed after they wrote a tribute track for the ElektroStat festival, after which a Bunkertracks compilation appearance led to their Alfa Matrix signing. The duo’s debut album, “We Are Kant Kino – You Are Not”, appeared in 2010. It was followed by the “LRSBSS EP” on April 15, 2012, then the second full-length “Father Worked In Industry” on February 22, 2013. “Father Worked In Industry” was mixed and mastered by Claus Larsen of Leaether Strip. That release also produced the download singles “Just For The Comfort Of Sleep EP” on March 26, 2013 and “Ich Liebe Katarina Witt EP” on November 22, 2013. While working toward the third album, the band previewed new material with the teaser “Life” in February 2016. While working on a new album, they self-released the Motörhead/Kraftwerk hybrid “We Are The Roadcrew (Robots)” on December 16, 2016, ahead of “Kopfkino”, which was released on Alfa Matrix on January 13, 2017. In May 2017, Alfa Matrix built the first “Matrix:Reb00ted” volume around Kant Kino remixes. The duo later appeared on the Coldkill vs Kant Kino EP “Silent Morning” in 2018, released the Depeche Mode cover single “Pimpf and Touch Faith” in September 2019, and self-released “Enough! (Demo)” on June 30, 2022. Kenneth Fredstie in the meantime mastered “Face The Beat: Session 3” and Kant Kino contributed “Ich Liebe Katarina Witt (Video Edit)” and “Life (No Fucking Guitars Edit)” to the Face The Beat series. They also contributed a remix for Modulo One’s “No Way to Win”, and remixed the Side-Line charity single “Ukraina” in December 2022. In February 2026, Kant Kino returned with “Rodney: End-State Variations”, followed by the fourth album “Echoes Of The End”, reviewed above.

items.body: Add a viola, and the whole world changes. On Stella Maris, Pavia post-rockers Tristan de Cunha become a trio, thanks to Nicolò Vara, which moves their already orchestral sound to the realm of the majestic. Now in their tenth year, the band is still making waves, and these waves are larger than any that came before. The album is inspired by the followers of Our Lady Star of the Sea (as approved by the Catholic Church). One can see Mary on the cover, shrouded in mystery, the guiding star for those at sea. Through wind and storm, perils within and perils without, her prayers and those of her supplicants guide seafarers home. This is a great theme for a post-rock suite, allowing for peaks and valleys, high drama on the open seas, and grand spiritual themes. The album works best played as a single piece, unfolding as a suite. The opening notes are like a ship’s horn, cutting through the fog, stopping and restarting, underlining the tension. Vara enters swiftly like a tumultuous sea. The drummer adds a pulse. And then suddenly the ship pushes into gentler, ambient seas. Cymbals shimmer, the guitar refracts, the viola offers a meditation. And all this in the prelude alone! One barely notices as the piece tips into the title track, which bleeds reflection and even remorse in long, rolling tones: an early emotional highlight. To listen is to think of three sets of parties: the sailors, possibly lost at sea; the people left behind to wonder at wait; and the third, divine party, to whom both prior sets petition. The ominous “A Tidal Wave Shall Push Them to the Light” implies two kinds of light: safety and salvation, although death may lie between. The wave never breaks, but remains a constant shadow, ignoring nature’s laws, demanding divine intervention. After this, the album enters a zone of abstraction, like the dark imaginings of a fitful sleep, the sailors unaware of their fate, tortured by nightmares. The ship begins to steady in “Wound,” implying the wounds and thus the mercy of Christ: by his wounds we were healed. The spiritual associations are cemented in “The Veil” with the arrival of a subdued yet powerful choir. The Star of the Sea has intervened! This is the set’s high water mark, to which all builds and from which all subsides. When the strings enter, the song dives straight to the heart. In “Continuum,” the ship sets a course for home. For a decade, guitarist Francesco Vara and drummer Luca Scotti have been sailing the high seas alone. Nicolò Vara is a steadying force, echoing the bolstering presence of the divine. The hull is now stronger, the sails more flexible, the ship more confident in the storm. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Mind Maps 7 stands as another richly rewarding chapter in an extraordinary body of electronic music—one that continues to push gently at the boundaries of ambient, downtempo and sample-based composition without ever losing its sense of warmth or wonder. Long may these maps continue to unfold, pointing listeners towards the kind of electronic music that still feels capable of surprising, transporting and quietly reshaping the landscape around it. FSOL’s discography does not simply evolve; it mutates   There are few artists in electronic music who have remained as resolutely unknowable as The Future Sound of London. They are the embodiment of an enigma. For more than thirty years Garry Cobain and Brian Dougans have operated as both pioneers and outliers, continually reshaping their own vocabulary through an ever-expanding catalogue of albums, EPs, archives and aliases. While countless contemporaries became defined by genres they helped create, FSOL have consistently resisted taxonomy, preferring intuition over orthodoxy and exploration over repetition. Their discography does not simply evolve; it mutates. Part of that mystery has always been embedded in their process. FSOL have rarely offered the listener an easy route map. Names, identities, boundaries and explanations are often blurred or deliberately withheld, allowing the music to exist first as an experience rather than as a product. In an age where everything is indexed, categorised and instantly explained, their continued commitment to ambiguity feels almost radical. The work arrives as a place to enter, not merely an object to consume. “In an age where everything is indexed, categorised and instantly explained, their continued commitment to ambiguity feels almost radical. The work arrives as a place to enter, not merely an object to consume.” ~Will Wonks History, however, tends to return to one moment. “Papua New Guinea” remains the unavoidable touchstone—not because it was their first great work, but because it captured electronic music standing on the threshold of possibility. Emerging from Britain’s bleep-and-clonk years, in parallel with Warp‘s formative identity and the rapid mutation of acid house, it proposed an altogether different future. Built from the haunting vocal of Dead Can Dance‘s “Dawn of the Iconoclast,” the cavernous bassline of Meat Beat Manifesto‘s “Radio Babylon” and additional textures from Circuit‘s “Shelter Me,” FSOL transformed familiar source material into something wholly original. Breakbeats displaced rigid four-to-the-floor momentum, ambient textures sat alongside uncompromising low-end pressure, while melody became both emotional and transportive. Toughness and tenderness occupied the same space without contradiction. Its influence is difficult to overstate. In much the same way that Talk Talk inadvertently sketched the blueprint for post-rock, “Papua New Guinea” suggested that dance music could become something beyond the dancefloor. It pointed towards the seed of what we now know as IDM, planting an idea that electronic music could be cerebral, emotional, fractured and exploratory without losing its physical connection to rhythm. From there, its influence would echo through jungle, intelligent techno, ambient, trip hop, breakbeat, chill-out, broken beat and countless hybrid forms that defined the decade. Whether directly or indirectly, it helped legitimize experimentation as a central impulse within electronic music rather than a curious diversion from it. A living organism, continually rewriting itself :: Alongside A Guy Called Gerald‘s “Voodoo Ray,” LFO‘s “LFO,” and Orbital‘s “Chime,” “Papua New Guinea” stands as one of those genuinely era-defining recordings that crystallized the cultural optimism of an impending post-Thatcher Britain. These were not merely club records. They reflected a generation discovering new communities, new aesthetics and new ways of imagining itself beyond the orthodoxies of the preceding decade. As ever, those radical impulses would eventually be absorbed into the machinery of mainstream culture, their once-disruptive edges softened through repetition and commodification. Yet the original spark remains unmistakable. To trace the genealogy of contemporary electronic music is, sooner or later, to arrive at The Future Sound of London. “Papua New Guinea” is more than a classic; it is an archetype, a permanent timestamp marking the moment electronic music realized just how expansive its vocabulary could become. “I’m attempting to describe something deeply that exists most completely as sculptured sound. Music, such as we have gifted here, at its most powerful, escapes the boundaries of moribund explanation.” ~Will Wonks As we move through the fourth decade since that breakthrough, Mind Maps 7 finds Cobain and Dougans turning their attention towards the work of others, continuing to reinterpret and reshape electronic music through the unmistakable FSOL lens. The archive is not a museum; it is a living organism, continually rewriting itself. Opening with clocolan, the collection sees FSOL reworking material by Jack Dangers as Meat Beat Manifesto, Humanoid—the long-running Brian Dougans alias—Pye Corner Audio, the inimitable cable.percussion, Plaid, Canopy of Stars, Ruxpin, Heogen, Sundial Aeon, Syl Kougaï, Christ., and Pentagrams Of Discordia. These are not conventional remixes so much as acts of transformation. Familiar structures are dismantled, atmospheres are reimagined and fragments are repositioned, while the essential character of each source remains just visible beneath the surface. Across familiar territories and unexpected detours, breaks cut and shuffle, atmospheres touch, fracture and transform. Acts of transformation :: The sublime reworking of Plaid‘s heartbeating “Reindeer” arrives as the standout for me, although that conclusion undoubtedly carries its own resonant bias as a lifelong fan of their magical oeuvre. Yet there is no noticeable drop in quality across the entire collection. Ultimately, there are limits to this same language when I’m attempting to describe something deeply that exists most completely as sculptured sound. Music, such as we have gifted here, at its most powerful, escapes the boundaries of moribund explanation. Perhaps that is why FSOL continue to endure as a trustworthy creative force while some of their contemporaries have found comfort in routine or the familiar pull of nostalgia. Their music has never sought definitive answers, only fresh routes through familiar terrain, treating every ending as the beginning of another possibility. Mind Maps 7 is another reminder that exploration, curiosity and reinvention remain fundamental to both the practice of being human and the act of making art. More importantly, it stands as another richly rewarding chapter in an extraordinary body of electronic music—one that continues to push gently at the boundaries of ambient, downtempo and sample-based composition without ever losing its sense of warmth or wonder. Long may these maps continue to unfold, pointing listeners towards the kind of electronic music that still feels capable of surprising, transporting and quietly reshaping the landscape around it. items.body: Biogenes Resources is a testament to what a new generation of Russian electronic artists would do. The hope and whimsy that permeate the album hark back to a time of potential, where possibilities stretched across the many time zones of the vast Eastern land. In this reproduction, using the original MIDI files, the past reminds us of both the preciousness of our freedom of expression and that such expression can never be stifled. An expansive and playful brand of electronics Biogenes Resources by Novel 23   In some strange twist of history, the Soviet Union seems almost closer now than it did in 1997. Russia has returned a society where silence is the expectation. The hope, or the supposed hope, that came in 1991 has faded as a new form of repression has taken hold. Despite this, there were years of musical rejuvenation. Electronic music bloomed. Talent that had taken root now had the freedom to scatter their sounds. Labels like Art-Tek were seminal in this movement with homegrown artists offering brand new ideas and energy. Founded by Roman Belavkin, aka Solar X, and Yura Moorush, Art-Tek attracted a new generation of music machinists. Names like Ambidextrous, EU, Fizzarum and Novel 23 became part of the family as a smattering of CD and vinyl slowly became available. You’d have to have had your ear to the ground to have come across the releases, but the artists involved spread their wings to labels like City Centre Offices and Lo Recordings while also inspiring and appearing on contemporary imprints like SEALT. Russian musicians have found it difficult to distribute their music as they once did, current sanctions meaning that Bandcamp cannot be used to sell. The brief light of freedom has been consumed by shadow. Nevertheless, pinpricks of hope still shine through. Novel 23, Roman Belousov, has decided to return, to return to his very beginnings. In 1997 his debut album came out on Art-Tek, one of the label’s first releases. Biogenes Resources originally appeared as a cassette tape, Soviet analog machines employed to create an expansive and playful brand of electronics. Fast forward thirty years, Belousov has remade the entire album using the same equipment. Art-Tek founder, Solar X, recalls that “this was the first music Roman produced I remember, he began writing it in 1996 after we met, and I encouraged him to buy Soviet synths. One of the main instruments there was Electronica EM-25”. It is this very same machine that has been dusted off to recreate the eleven works of the collection. A narrative of nature runs through the album :: Novel 23’s first release, the album is filled with charm and the innocence of a young artist. For those not familiar with Belousov’s work, immediate comparisons would be the likes of Bochum Welt or CiM. Here, the mood is somewhat more subdued. Soft synth-lines swirl below acid globules and brittle beats in the opening “Dawn Without Hope.” An off-kilter melody bends and bulges in the fragile “Clear Sky” before the meandering brightness of “Not Caught Fish.” A narrative of nature runs through the album with track titles such as “Transparent Brook” and “Light Storm Cloud.” Each work holds the seed of the talent that Novel 23 would become. The absorbing and unsettling quality of “Cool Sun Rays”, the texture and warmth of “Thick Mist in Lowland” and understated elegance of “Sunset for Rain” resonate as a precursor to Belousov’s later audio explorations. “Change of Wind & Temperature” is the most immersive offering of the album. Brimming with enthusiasm, flashes of the later Novel 23 sound and style come to the fore. Biogenes Resources is a testament to what a new generation of Russian electronic artists would do. The hope and whimsy that permeate the album hark back to a time of potential, where possibilities stretched across the many time zones of the vast Eastern land. In this reproduction, using the original MIDI files, the past reminds us of both the preciousness of our freedom of expression and that such expression can never be stifled. Biogenes Resources is available on Art-Tek. [Bandcamp] Biogenes Resources by Novel 23The post Novel 23 :: Biogenes Resources (Art-Tek) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Human Music: Live Improvisations I serves as both a statement and a philosophy. What I hear is a collection of live performance recordings, each about 6-7 minutes long, one player/performer using layers and loop technology to play many instruments at once in a live setting, creating classical flavored music improvisations and instrumental expressions with haunting vocals that are entirely without word content, just emotional tones that bend and transmit. Emotional responses that define genuine human expression Human Music: Live Improvisations I by Jessica Roch   Jessica Roch brings her insightful studio mixing skills to these improvised multi-instrumental tours de force, drawn from performances captured between 2022 and 2025 in concert halls, intimate venues, and assembly rooms across England. Human Music: Live Improvisations I is a document of spontaneity, vulnerability, and presence that was written, recorded, produced, arranged, and mixed, as well as performed live by Jessica Roch on violin, synth, vocals, pianos, vibraphone, many pedals and (many) electronics. In this six track anthology the audiences are breathless, each piece unfolds in real time, free from predetermined outcomes, embracing the subtle imperfections, fleeting decisions, and emotional responses that define genuine human expression. She also created the cover art, an eye-catching expression of photographic compositing and imagery, with the album’s physical graphic design and layout by zakè. Human Music serves as both a statement and a philosophy. What I hear is a collection of live performance recordings, each about 6-7 minutes long, one player/performer using layers and loop technology to play many instruments at once in a live setting, creating classical flavored music improvisations and instrumental expressions with haunting vocals that are entirely without word content, just emotional tones that bend and transmit. Human Music, to me, describes how the focus is on truth and insight. There is risk taking, being honest and thorough, as well as staying nimble. These performances were each invented on the fly. These recordings are not polished constructions assembled from endless revisions, but living moments captured as they happened, shaped by the atmosphere of the room, the energy of the audience, and the artist’s instinct in the moment. There is never any AI present here. Living moments captured as they happened :: In an era increasingly shaped by automation and algorithmic creation, Human Music celebrates the irreplaceable qualities of live performance: intuition, risk, connection, and the profound beauty found in uncertainty. “London Live Session, Oct. ’25” opens with a piano, which communicates empathy and intuition, never any urgency, just easy relaxing floating on the infinite sea, eased by repeating ethereal voices that haunt like a night-drawn candle would. At “Threadsafe, King’s Cross, Dec. ’24” there are flutes flying about all over the place, flickering and fluttering, followed by a robust violin session. We float around nicely for part of eternity while the heavenly vocal choir echoes somewhere above, and soon the cathedral is filled with so many voices, legions coming back together as one. The program at “St. John on Bethnal Green, Oct. ’24” starts with vocals and that big cathedral sound, in time a choir builds and soon the hot violin arrives and weaves around the choir refrains. The feeling is satisfying and peaceful, with a feeling of intimate intricacy. “A masterpiece of depth and warmth, wrapped in strange beauty surely evoked by classical wandering spirits.” ~Robin B. James “Liquid Light Session One, Oct. ’22” starts off when the pianos interact, a violin is plucked delicately and very subtly, within and without. The vibraphone grooves in, sly and lean, forming a nice multilayered atmosphere of instruments and vocal presence. Later, at “Liquid Light Session Two, Oct. ’22” it feels like water is reflecting multicolored light, flickering and exploding as shadows silently signal a response. The violin somehow changes the feeling, and ghosts are musically gesturing in the background. For the final track, “Howard Assembly Room, Leeds, Jun. ’24” we start from plucked violin strings, layering behind a bright bowed story teller, leading into some fancy violin playing. This comes after as well as during the vocal moments, adding many serious details. Some are a little dark, perhaps slightly sad. Of course there are no words, the voices that join in next have a teasing warble, and the rare elvish fairies nearly yodel. Soon the violin becomes the main thing, finishing with a warm synth-orchestra memory invoking assemblage. Water is reflecting multicolored light, flickering and exploding :: Jessica Roch is a London based, award winning composer, multi instrumentalist, sound designer, and improviser. In 2025, she received a Composer Spotlight Award at the Production Music Awards. She has recently performed at Cafe OTO and is a co-founder and director of The London Ambient Orchestra. Her solo work moves fluidly across genres, weaving ambient and electronic textures with elements of minimalism, jazz, folk, and experimental music. A classically trained violinist and pianist, Jessica creates music for film, games, and contemporary media, while also collaborating as a session musician with artists including Super Furry Animals. Jessica‘s composition Pandemonium: Music for Parakeets, was created as part of a cross disciplinary artistic collaboration, and was featured at The Design Museum as part of the Artificial exhibition, where it was on display throughout the summer season. Recently speaking about her debut album on Past Inside the Present, Jessica clarifies her intention. “This album is an unambiguous protest and rejection of AI-generated “music.” Human Music: Live Improvisations I, is imperfect, it is raw and it is unpredictable. That is the beauty of live improvisation. It is innately human.” “This album is an unambiguous protest and rejection of AI-generated “music.” Human Music: Live Improvisations I, is imperfect, it is raw and it is unpredictable. That is the beauty of live improvisation. It is innately human.” ~Jessica Roch Beautifully curated from an extensive collection of live performances, the album was mixed by Jessica herself and mastered with remarkable sensitivity by James Bernard at Ambient Mountain House. Together they preserve the immediacy and emotional depth of each performance while allowing every nuance, resonance, and breath of the room to remain intact. The result is a deeply personal body of work that stands as both an artistic statement and a testament to the enduring power of human creativity. Human Music: Live Improvisations I was shrinkwrapped, pressed, manufactured, and assembled in Ontario, Canada, with an edition of 200, glass-mastered, silkscreen printed CDs housed in a 4-panel, 300g satin cardstock Digipak with a clear cd tray. Human Music: Live Improvisations I is a masterpiece of depth and warmth, wrapped in strange beauty surely evoked by classical wandering spirits. This four-track mini album ismade up of covers of Pink Floyd, the Who, King Crimson, and Flower Travellin' Band, and thisexcellent selection definitely predisposes for a beautiful psychedelic experiment to unfold. I don'tknow if is the shorter length or the better production, but 'Lime and Limpid Green' just feelstighter and more cohesive than the duo's debut studio release. Their unhinged psych-rock side is onfull display here, with both Les Claypool and Sean Lennon providing vocals alongside their usualinstrumental duties, as was the case with 'Monolith of Phobos'. And speaking of this album, myimpression of it was that the stronger Primus influence, which is completely missing from this EP,had allowed for somewhat of a stylistic jumble.However, the versions of 'Astronomy Domine' and 'The Court of the Crimson King' played here areexcellent to the core, while the covers of 'Satori' and 'Boris the Spider' are not mere playthroughsof the original songs, but well-done modern renditions that are fun and trippy. There is somethingdelirious about this four-track release, and I would say it is highly recommended for fans of spacerock, neo-psychedelia, and prog.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Rain Dances' is the fifth studio album from English band Camel, originally released by Decca in1977. This is the follow-up to 'The Snow Goose' and 'Moonmadness', both of which are albums I'venever been overly crazy about, hence my general lack of appreciation for this period of the band'shistory. Nevertheless, 'Rain Dances' is an interesting offering, it being the first Camel album withRichard Sinclair of Caravan on bass and vocals, and with King Crimson's original sax player MelCollins, whose contribution to the album in question is unfortunately fairly minimal, butsufficiently memorable. Sinclair's influence (and perhaps the overall appeal of the CanterburyScene) is felt on this Camel album much more than on any of the band's preceding releases. Whetherit be through the poppier melodies, or the covert proneness to jazzy experiments, 'Rain Dances' is adelightful little album that in my ears is just not on par with classics like 'Mirage' or the self-titled debut LP.It is also worth noting that about half of 'Rain Dances' is made up of instrumentals, whereas R.Sinclair handles the lead vocals on three of the album tracks, and Andrew Latimer on just one. Andso, the overall impression I get from this record is that of a slightly uneven work that attempts topresent itself as eclectic but fails to do so by jumping from jazzier prog to straightforward pop-rock somewhat abruptly. Side one of 'Rain Dances' is the more accessible one, by the way, withopening track 'First Light' delivering a lush, dreamy soundscape in the opening section, whereasPeter Bardens' gorgeous synth becomes more prominent later on. We also hear Mel Collins interveningbeautifully towards the end of this piece. 'Metrognome' is a better-known song from this album - afusion-inspired prog number with soft-spoken vocals and laid-back atmosphere. 'Tell Me' is a songthat is melancholic to the point of being sombre, while 'Highways of the Sun' is nothing more than apoppy tune with unremarkable vocals.Side two start off more promisingly with 'Unevensong', which is one of the least funereal-soundingsongs on 'Rain Dances', and this is definitely a compliment here. On a side note, its instrumentalmiddle section is truly enjoyable. 'One of These Days...' captures a vital guitar solo from AndrewLatimer, one of the few on the album, but an undeniably tasteful one, while 'Elke' and the titletrack work well as pastoral passages through space and time. 'Skylines', on the other hand, is aproggy instrumental with excellent performances all along, and one of the more memorable entries on'Rain Dances'.Generally this is a mild album, parts of which are strong, while others are very mediocre. What Imostly miss here is the epic nature of the band's earlier compositions; the addition of RichardSinclair and Mel Collins should have influenced this record differently, I believe, but at the sametime it is not a bad offering.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — I saw their 2024 debut pass by and did not or could not latch onto it for further perusal, but who else than my revered prog colleague and friend Lazland to set me on the right path by reading his glowing review of this sophomore work, that finally ordered me to hunt this one down. Also being in a duet band structure myself, I more than just understand the benefits of synergy between two people with common goals and outlooks. Large bands can have ego problems that can pollute the political climate and force argument, dismissal or even surrender. Seemingly, Poli Elizondo and Guillermo Garcia have created an artistic musical relationship where the guidelines are clearly set from the start, each one involved in stimulating the other and thus, finding stylistic common ground. The title track sets the cinematographic tone with an extensive (and longest piece here), introducing the multiple strengths of each musician, Poli is an accomplished bass and electric guitar player, while Guillermo owns a seductive voice that oozes either hushed or passionate sentiments (at times, I heard a bit of Peter Murphy, in less gothic tones), and adorns the compositions with skillful keyboard spines, leaving plenty of room for broad flamboyance when required. The atmosphere is melancholic and tragic, the lyrical message is one of the usual hardships associated with life on the blue planet, you know, freedom, the endless pursuit of happiness and the quest for something better than what has already been acquired. As tasty as the opening piece was, "Rising Sand" raises (excuse the pun) the sonic threshold with a pulverizing bass and drum connection, the flaunting four strings unafraid to boldly wander into side dunes towards the end, Guillermo's vocal ramping up the vigour with a resonating sense of reality. On "A Dark Place", there is a ton of gravitas in the overall sombre delivery, practically reminiscent of Mamouna -era Bryan Ferry, the crushed voice severely desolate, the distant electric guitar introspectively searching for panacea, the piano shining like ghostly ivory and a yearning for any form of understanding. Perhaps only then will the sun flicker through. Somehow. "Turmoil" follows suite, a piano-led dirge, Guillermo surely singing from his knees, a glittering guitar plea that explodes with restrained intensity overhead. Three final pieces, each in the 6-7-minute range, implies that this was purposefully constructed, as if a trio of chapters were necessary in order to survive. "Keep Breathing" comes across as particularly truculent, far from any hint of tropical paradise, actually the polar opposite. It has a quasi-Icelandic feel, a cold and barren melancholia counterbalanced by occasional geysers of infernal chanting, hell-fired guitar flashes out to decimate any remaining vegetation that may have survived. The definite acme is reached on the stupendous "Burn as One", a melody so intense, that within seconds, tears may start flowing. The impeccable groove is preciously maintained yet delves even deeper into the tragedy of emotional discord, the eternal obstacle the vast majority of humans often face, yearning for loving and being loved, at times a seemingly impossible task. Everything here services the anguish, from the hopeful piano chords, the churning organ interjection, the irritated elevation in the voice, a colossal choir finale and the pulsating rhythmic pounding throughout. Yes, time flies. This is playlist material, a love song for the ages, a stunning modern prog.Finally, the revelation arrives that being human means that in order to survive hardship, someone needs to move on, somehow, somewhere and sometime. "The Waiting Game" sends the message to keep the faith, not the public example, but that inner individual strength, the one that leads by principle, that makes our blood circulate and our lungs to breathe in the air. 'Its all about the journey, the waiting game is so long'! Put that in a loop and pray to it each and every day. An ear-opening discovery that satisfied the craving to understand the extremes of our own emotions, how easy/difficult it can be to go from one to the other. The idea is to find that moment when you stop, because you found the balance point. It's smack in the middle, and you will never fall off. Music can be a healing form of panacea. Muchas gracias Laz 4.5 Pink reveries

Maybe it's about a new period of life or rethinking life, which appears in a bright light. The sound of greatness and heritage fills the soul. Next, the listener hears a transition into a piano section, which creates the feeling of action and gradual movement. Afterward, a development into faster, more dynamic sound appears, and a sense of potential and growth is felt. Finally, the composition ends with a mysterious and hypnotic feeling.2) Captivated. The beginning immediately captures attention. Sleeping or dreaming, the listener seems to awaken from hypnosis. The image of someone inspired arises. He decides to take action in order to get his object of desire. There's a sense of enthusiasm and great effort to handle one's obsession, its nearness evokes a sense of greatness. But there is a confusion and perhaps disappointment, which are the finishing part. Realization and fatigue fill the ending of the composition.3) Target. A gradual deepening into something mysterious is replaced with soft sounds that prepare the listener for the next part. Its speed and instability induce the feeling of torments of the soul. Uncertainty creates a motive for searching the solution. Harsh sounds make a listener feel on alert, nudging the listener to keep searching and moving forward.4) Teach Me Your Statutes. This composition can make you feel deeply sad. The listener experiences mutual misunderstanding, disappointment, and desperation while listening to this. Though these are often seen as negative feelings, the strength and beauty of them cannot go unnoticed. In the second part, there is development. Transition to hardly notable sounds and thrill create the tension and anxious atmosphere. Perhaps the beginnings of love or commitment are the most fitting context to experience this feeling.5) Loneliness-Bringing Power.The composition starts gradually, preparing the listener for something important. The slow melody creates a comforting atmosphere. It transitions into something unknown and challenging ? perhaps loneliness. It flows into taking on a challenge and a way to achieve something meaningful, bringing new discoveries and experiences. The denouement brings a sense of joy and happiness.6) Three Sunny Light Power. It motivates to enjoy life and to be in the moment. This part ends with the sound of bells. The bells give a final polish to what has been achieved and bring the feeling of satisfaction.7) Resilience. The soft sounds gently awaken the listener in the beginning of the composition. The atmosphere conveys calm, stability, and peace of mind. Subtle hints of mystery transit the listener to loading into realization and meaning. It then gives way to a graceful finale. The feeling of probable resilience can inspire confidence and a quiet sense of satisfaction.8) Silence Is Waiting. It starts in a similar way to the previous composition. There is a hypnotic quality here as well. It creates a perfect atmosphere to meditate and clear thoughts. A sense of peace comes over the listener. The cosmic sounds evoke space, making the listener feel weightless and far removed from earthly concerns.Each composition on the album felt like a chapter in an emotional and spiritual narrative ? sometimes uplifting, sometimes sorrowful, but always sincere. This album offers more than sound; it offers space for reflection, imagination, and inner movement.

items.body: Review by Stefano61 — There is a particular kind of return that has nothing to do with nostalgia and everything to do with stubbornness.Opus Avantra were born in the Veneto in the early seventies out of an idea rather than a line-up: AVANguardia and TRAdizione, avant-garde and tradition, welded into a single word by the soprano Donella Del Monaco, the pianist and composer Alfredo Tisocco, the philosopher Giorgio Bisotto and the producer Renato Marengo. Their 1974 debut, universally known as Introspezione, remains one of the strangest objects in the entire Italian catalogue of that decade, a record that belongs to progressive rock mostly because nobody could think where else to file it, and which earned the group a place on the Nurse With Wound list among the true outsiders of European music.Lord Cromwell Plays Suite For Seven Vices followed in 1975, then long silences broken by Strata in 1989, Lyrics in 1995, and Venetia et Anima in 2003. Sixteen years later, on the fourteenth of January 2019, Rosa Rosae appeared, produced once again by Renato Marengo, the same man who had produced the debut forty five years earlier, under the artistic direction of Tisocco. Whatever else it is, it is a circle closing.The record is credited to Donella Del Monaco, Paolo Troncon and the Opus Avantra Ensemble, and that order of names is accurate. Del Monaco writes all the texts and sings them, moving between Latin, Italian and French with a delivery that comes from the conservatory and from a family where the surname Del Monaco meant something before she ever recorded a note. Troncon composes, arranges and directs, and his training is classical and contemporary rather than rock: he writes in polyrhythmic and contrapuntal forms rather than in verses and choruses, which is precisely why this is not a pop record wearing a costume.The ensemble is Mauro Martello on flutes, saxophones and duduk, Laura Balbinot on cello, Andrea De Nardi on keyboards and Giorgio Cedolin on drums, expanded by accordions, a second cello, tenor saxophones and percussion. The guest list reads like a summit of the Italian seventies: Tony Esposito, who had already played on the 1974 debut, Lino Vairetti of Osanna, Jenny Sorrenti of Saint Just, and Alberto Radius of Formula 3, whose contribution here now carries an unintended weight, since he died in February 2023.The theme is the rose and therefore love, declined between sacred and profane, devotion and desire, with the two poles deliberately confused and sometimes inverted. It is a concept album in the old and serious sense of the term, not a suite with a title stuck on afterwards.A word on sequencing, because it matters. The 2019 CD ran nine pieces and opened with the accordion led lyricism of Nuvole Bianche. The later vinyl edition carries eleven, fully resequenced, adding the previously unreleased L'Angelo Caduto, restoring Aurea Lyra in its original version rather than the CD reworking, and bringing Sceleratus back as a closing reprise. That order opens with the darkest music on the record and holds the warmth in reserve, which strikes me as the truer shape of the work.The track-by-track below follows the vinyl sequence.- Sceleratus: the severest thing here, sung in Latin, with Lino Vairetti's powerful Mediterranean baritone answering Del Monaco line for line. Exorcism and mysticism circling each other. As an opening statement it warns you immediately that this will not be comfortable listening.- Mandala: an instrumental in all but atmosphere, built on the interlocking percussion of Tony Esposito and Gabriele Bruzzolo over Troncon's piano, with Andrea Martin's tenor saxophone tracing long lines above. The most openly rhythmic piece on the album, and the clearest link back to the debut.- Aurea Lyra (original version): piano by Dimitri Romano, accordion, cello and percussion, a chamber ensemble rather than a band. The original reading is drier and less upholstered than the one issued on CD, and it gains from that.- Pi Greco: the shortest and most abstract passage, a piece of pure construction whose title tells you everything about the intention. It functions as a hinge rather than a destination.- Rosa Rosae: the title track, and the centre of gravity. Tenor saxophone, accordion, cello and piano weave around Del Monaco's voice in what is closest here to a genuine song, though the counterpoint never relaxes into accompaniment. The rose as flower and as rosary, both at once.- L'Angelo Caduto: the previously unreleased piece, and no mere appendix. The fallen angel is the natural counterpart to the diabolic material of Sceleratus, and it sits squarely inside the concerns of the record rather than beside them. Its absence from the CD now feels like an omission.- Nuvole Bianche: the accordion of Mirko Satto and Troncon's piano, the most immediately beautiful thing on the album and the piece that once opened it. Placed here, deep into the second side, it arrives as relief rather than as invitation, which suits it better.- Cyrcles: Alberto Radius plugs in and plays, unmistakably, with that liquid seventies tone set against Tommaso Troncon's tenor saxophone. A deliberate homage to the decade the group came from, and now an elegy as well.- Vento Del Nord: written by Del Monaco with Mauro Martello, and the one duet on the record, with Jenny Sorrenti. Two voices that could easily have fought each other and instead lean together. Quietly the most moving few minutes here.- Ineffabile Realt�: Troncon alone at the piano. After everything that has preceded it, the austerity feels earned rather than imposed.- Sceleratus (Reprise): the Latin returns, briefly, and the door closes on the same shadow it opened with.Rosa Rosae asks something of the listener, and it does not pretend otherwise. Those who come to Opus Avantra hoping for the corrosive weirdness of Introspezione will find this more measured, more written, more willing to be beautiful; the fracture lines of 1974 have been smoothed by fifty years of thinking about the same problem. There are moments where the chamber writing verges on the decorous, and the abstract interludes will lose the impatient.Yet the ambition is intact and entirely unfashionable: a group that has spent half a century refusing to choose between the conservatory and the rock stage, still refusing, still finding new ways to hold the two apart without letting either win. Del Monaco's voice has darkened and gained gravity, Troncon's writing gives it architecture worthy of it, and the guests are used as colours rather than as selling points.This is a late chapter, and it knows it, but it is a rich one and it belongs on the shelf beside the records that made the name. An excellent album from a band that never learned how to be ordinary.My rating: 4/5.Bassano del Grappa (Italy), August 2026
